paragraphs.text: Plastic was once celebrated as a miracle material: cheap, light and almost indestructible. Its durability, however, has become its greatest problem. Since the 1950s, more than eight billion tonnes of plastic have been produced, and only around 9% of it has ever been recycled. A large proportion has ended up in the environment, where it does not biodegrade but gradually breaks into smaller and smaller pieces.

Fragments smaller than five millimetres are known as microplastics. Some are produced deliberately, such as the tiny beads once added to toothpaste and facial scrubs, many of which have now been banned. Most, however, come from the breakdown of larger items: bottles, fishing nets and bags are broken up by sunlight and waves. Another major source is synthetic clothing. A single wash of a polyester garment can release hundreds of thousands of fibres, which are too small to be caught by most wastewater treatment plants.

Microplastics have now been found almost everywhere scientists have looked: in Arctic sea ice, in the deepest ocean trenches, in table salt and in tap water. In 2022, researchers in the Netherlands reported detecting plastic particles in human blood for the first time. Their presence in the food chain is particularly well documented in marine life. Small organisms such as plankton mistake the particles for food, and these organisms are in turn eaten by fish, seabirds and eventually humans.

What this means for human health remains unclear. Laboratory studies have shown that very high concentrations of microplastics can damage cells and cause inflammation, but the levels used in such experiments are often far higher than those to which people are actually exposed. Scientists are also concerned about the chemicals that plastics contain or absorb from the surrounding water, some of which are known to interfere with hormones. Most researchers agree that more long-term studies are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

Removing microplastics from the oceans is virtually impossible because of their size and the vast area over which they are spread. Efforts are therefore focused on preventing new plastic from entering the environment. Measures include charges on plastic bags, which reduced their use by more than 80% in some countries, improved waste collection in developing nations and filters for washing machines. In 2022, member states of the United Nations agreed to begin negotiating a legally binding global treaty on plastic pollution.
